title: Cost II: Economies of Scale, Learning, and Experience Curves
keyQuestion: How does a firm get a scale cost advantage? What is the real reason Tesla beats Ford and GM?

reading.name: Economies of Scale: scale, learning, and experience (brief)

slides: S8 deck 'Cost Advantage' (41): Aldi anchor, sources of cost advantage, scale and scope, pizza example, Netflix Q1-Q5 model answers, scale curves, scale/learning/experience table, EVs (Tesla, Rivian, Lucid, Ford, GM)

framework.name: Scale vs. learning vs. experience
framework.summary: 'Economies of scale' names three different mechanisms that produce near-identical cost curves. Scale is about a current RATE (output per period; a property of your configuration). Learning is about a HISTORY (cumulative output; a property of your past). The experience curve is BCG's deliberate bundle of everything that happens to total cost as volume accumulates — and a prescription to buy share.

components.name: Scale economies (the rate)
components.what: Average cost vs. output per period. Build bigger, run longer, spread fixed cost over more units this quarter. Reversible: cut the rate and it's gone the same day.

components.name: Six scale mechanisms
components.what: 1) Geometry (cost ∝ capacity^0.6 for whole plants → ~24% lower unit capital cost per doubling). 2) Indivisibility (blast furnace, sales force, codebase, Super Bowl ad — fixed across a range). 3) Specialization (Smith's pin factory: 4,800 pins/person/day vs. <20; limited by the extent of the market). 4) Bargaining (weakest: Wright's purchased material 88% and raw material 95% curves vs. labor 80%). 5) Statistics (square-root law: pooling n independent locations cuts safety stock to 1/√n). 6) Demand-side scale (network effects raise WTP, don't lower cost; don't run out at MES; markets tip).

components.name: Minimum efficient scale (MES)
components.what: The smallest output at which average cost is essentially minimized. Industry structure depends on MES relative to market size, and on the cost penalty below MES (shoes 0.2% of demand → fragmented; autos 21-30% → three to five producers).

components.name: Plant vs. firm scale (the merger-memo warning)
components.what: Real scale economies are mostly inside a plant. Firm-level economies are small (Bain: 1-2%; none of 12 industries showed moderate firm effects) and diseconomies are well documented (Zenger on R&D).

components.name: Learning (the history)
components.what: Cost vs. cumulative output. Wright 1936: 80% curve for direct LABOR only (exponent 0.322), cumulative-average not unit; the whole airplane curve flattens from 83% to 90%. Largely irreversible, though it decays.

components.name: Learning-curve arithmetic
components.what: Y = a·X^−b; progress ratio s = 2^−b, b = −log₂ s; cut per doubling = 1 − s; doublings d = log₂(X₂/X₁), cost ratio = s^d; fit s = (Y₂/Y₁)^(1/d); doublings to close a gap d = ln(C_follower/C_leader) ÷ (−ln s), then required volume = today's × 2^d. Ask which convention 'learning rate' means (s or 1−s).

components.name: Experience curve (BCG doctrine)
components.what: All costs 'of every kind' in constant dollars vs. accumulated volume, 20-30% per doubling, 'without limit'. Prescription: 'Market share must be maintained at all costs as long as growth rate exceeds the anticipated rate of return'; price new products 'as low as necessary to dominate'.

components.name: Why they can't be separated
components.what: Pure geometry (24% per doubling of plant capacity) sits inside BCG's 20-30% band; in a growing industry plant capacity and cumulative volume double together, so no cost series distinguishes them. When separated (Thompson's Liberty ships), learning's share was small (~70% capital deepening; ~5% residual).

components.name: The three diagnostic questions
components.what: 1) Is cost falling because of how much I make this period or how much I've ever made? 2) Would it survive a year at half the volume? 3) Can my competitor read about it (does learning leak)?

terms.def: Brief: a relationship between average cost and output per period. Slides: a reduction in cost per unit due to increased efficiency as the number of goods produced increases (technical, managerial, financial/marketing, network economies).

A reduction in average total cost from increasing the number of DIFFERENT goods produced — from sharing R&D, marketing/brand, distribution, retail relationships (P&G-style), or technology, customer accounts, fulfilment, last mile, Prime, forecasting (Amazon).
Brief: cost vs. cumulative output (Wright: direct labor). Slides: labor costs per unit decrease with increases in volume due to learning.
BCG's representation of the relationship between cumulative volume and total product cost; bundles scale, learning and technical change.
Cost at 2X ÷ cost at X; an 80% curve leaves cost at 80% after each doubling (a 20% cut).
Smallest output at which average cost is essentially minimized.
Consolidating n independent locations leaves safety stock at 1/√n (sixteen into one → −75%); collapses if demands move together.
Whole-plant capital cost rises with capacity^0.6 (Chilton 1950): doubling capacity costs 1.52x, so unit capital cost falls to 0.758x (−24.2%).
Williamson's four: atmospheric consequences, bureaucratic insularity, incentive limits of employment, communication distortion. Brooks: n(n−1)/2 channels (50 people → 1,225).
Costs rising with experience: French nuclear construction costs rose (×3 Grubler; ~60% Komanoff) as reactor size grew.
Rivals pick up part of your learning (nuclear ~1/3; shipyards spillovers may exceed own learning) — it may be an industry public good you're paying for.

claims.claim: Scale is about a current rate; learning is about a history.
Most firms discover which one they had involuntarily, in a recession when demand drops.
What determines industry structure is not whether scale economies exist but the ratio of MES to market size.
Entry to the leading edge of chips rose ~14x in twenty years ($2bn → $28bn per fab) and the number of firms who can buy one fell from 18 to 3 — a scale story.
The 80% curve is not a law: Dutton & Thomas found progress ratios from 55% to 108% across 100+ studies.
Learning decays: Bongers finds only ~7% of Super Hornet experience retained year to year; a paused program does not resume where it stopped.

Texas Instruments priced the TI-99/4A down to $99 (and $49) on an experience curve it did not own; Commodore, vertically integrated into its own chips (MOS Technology), sat on a lower curve. TI lost $145M in 1983 and exited.

Ghemawat's conditions: wrong technology kills you regardless of volume; slow-doubling industries can't pay; forcing output can raise cost (TriStar); substitution destroys the accumulated base (cellophane). Du Pont TiO2: mechanics worked, demand didn't.
Rigidity: Ford cut Model T cost ~3/4 and took share 10% → 55%, then needed most of a year (~$200M) to retool for the Model A, handing the market to GM.
Learning lodges in people more than institutions (surgeon volume OR 0.29 vs. hospital 0.35); corporate size is not learning — hospital acquisitions made patient experience worse (−0.17 SD).
Blockbuster had size without scale economies; Netflix had scale economies before it had size.
Scale economies tell you average cost falls; they don't tell you who captures the surplus — rented inputs from concentrated suppliers leak the value upstream (Starz $30M → $300M).

failures.name: Calling size 'scale'
failures.what: Blockbuster: 9,000 stores, flat average cost — MES was one store.

failures.name: Firm-level scale claims in merger memos
failures.what: Evidence for firm-level economies is thin; diseconomies are documented.

failures.name: Experience doctrine as pricing rule
failures.what: Pricing ahead of cost on a curve you don't own (TI).

failures.name: Ignoring Ghemawat's conditions
failures.what: Wrong technology, slow doubling, forced output, substitution.

failures.name: Ignoring leakage and decay
failures.what: Your accumulated volume advantage is smaller than the model says.

caseFacts.fact: Blockbuster: 9,000+ stores and ~$6B revenue at the 2004 peak; each store replicated the full cost structure (lease, labor, local inventory); late fees ~$800M (~15% of revenue) in 2000; ~$1B spin-off debt; Total Access losing up to $400M/yr; bankrupt Sept 2010.
caseFacts.why: Size without scale economies: average cost per rental about the same for 9,000 stores as for 900.

caseFacts.fact: DVD-by-mail: one national inventory, ~60 distribution centers, 95% next-day by 2007, Cinematch steering to the back catalog (>half of queue adds from recommendations); subscribers 1M (2002) → 5M (2006) → ~10M (2008).
caseFacts.why: Fixed costs (website, recommendation system, DC network) spread over every subscriber; demand pooling raised utilization — a downward-sloping curve with a postage floor.

caseFacts.fact: Streaming: content and platform become fixed; AC = F/N + c with c a few cents — cost per subscriber halves with every doubling of N. At F = $17B: 10M subs → $1,700/yr ($142/mo); 50M → $340 ($28); 100M → $170 ($14); 200M → $85 ($7.10); 300M → $57 ($4.70). Breakeven on content alone at ~$12 ARPU needs ~118M subscribers.
caseFacts.why: The steepness is the whole story: small differences in N produce enormous differences in unit cost, and the leader's spend raises everyone's MES.

caseFacts.fact: Licensing leaked: Starz ~$30M/yr (2008) → Netflix offered $300M+ (2011) and Starz walked; 2019 reclamations (Disney; The Office $500M/5 yrs; Friends $425M/5 yrs).
caseFacts.why: Concentrated suppliers with hold-up power captured the value of Netflix's scale; originals = vertical integration into the input (cost certainty, global perpetual rights, exclusivity).
Seven times the spend, about the same unit cost; HBO couldn't match because of distribution (MVPDs), the parent's profit pool, and an organization calibrated to a linear schedule.
Fixed-cost leverage: cost share of revenue falls, margin rises as revenue grows against a fixed content base.

caseFacts.fact: Q3 2025: Netflix quarterly streaming operating profit $2.55B vs. Disney+/Hulu $352M, HBO Max $345M, Paramount+ $340M, Peacock −$217M.
caseFacts.why: Rivals sit far up the average-cost curve.

caseFacts.fact: Professor's scale curves: cost per subscriber per month 2006-2013 fit y = 181.61x^−0.297 (R² 0.95) → ~18% per doubling ('scale curve'); 2011-2025 ~4% ('experience curve').
caseFacts.why: The answer to the case's Assignment 1 — the curve flattens as Netflix reaches the bottom.

caseFacts.fact: EVs (2025): Tesla 9.0M cumulative, learning rate 7.4%, $46,978 cost per vehicle; Rivian 174k, 18.5%, $123,995, needs 4.7 doublings = 27x its output to date; Lucid 43k, 16.4%, $146,300, 6.4 doublings = 82x. Ford Model e: $4.8B EBIT loss on $6.7B revenue → $32k-57k loss per vehicle; GM est. $12k-18k loss. Tesla takes nearly half of US EV sales.
caseFacts.why: The real reason Tesla beats Ford and GM: cumulative EV volume on a NEW cost curve (battery, software, electrical architecture). Incumbents' scale sits in stamping, assembly and distribution; they have volume of the wrong kind.

strongAnalysis: How a firm gets a scale cost advantage: locate the fixed costs, find the unit at which cost is incurred (store vs. nation), measure the slope, and ask who appropriates the gains (S8 synthesis). Netflix moved costs from variable to fixed with each pivot, making each curve steeper, and then pushed MES beyond rivals by raising the content ante.

Test it with the brief's diagnostic: Netflix's advantage is scale (rate of subscribers), not learning — halve subscribers and cost per subscriber doubles. And it's supply-side, not a network effect: one subscriber's utility doesn't rise because another joins, so it's contestable by a rival willing to finance years of losses (as Netflix proved).

Tesla vs. Ford/GM: not 'better management' — it's which curve. EV cost falls with cumulative EV output (battery packs, software, architecture). Tesla's 9M cumulative units put it far down that curve; Rivian and Lucid learn faster (18.5%, 16.4%) but each doubling needs twice the volume (27x, 82x output to date — past a century at 2025 rates). Ford/GM have scale in the old curve. Two defensible escapes: stop competing on a dimension decided by cumulative volume, or reset the curve with a different process (S8 slide 31 notes).

Durability (Q5): for — rising fixed-cost ante (sports rights), new layers on the same base (ads, games, live), consolidation, suppliers need Netflix's checkbook again. Against — content is fixed but not sunk-once (paid every year), talent and rights holders capture rents, international ARPU ~1/3 of US flattens the revenue side, and YouTube/TikTok shift the basis of competition.

counter.argument: Netflix's advantage is differentiation (originals, brand, recommendation engine), not cost; Squid Game and Stranger Things are why people subscribe.
counter.response: Originals are the differentiation, but the reason Netflix can afford a library rivals can't is cost per subscriber: the same $17B costs it ~$57 per subscriber per year and costs a 41M-subscriber rival seven times that. Exclusivity and recommendations sit on top of a scale cost advantage (S8 slides 21, 23). Both sides of the wedge are moving — a preview of dual advantage (S11).

courseMap.text: Scale and learning are two of Porter's ten cost drivers (S7) and two of the three sources of cost leadership named in the generic strategies paper (scale, experience, structure). Contrast with Aldi's structural advantage (S8 synthesis). MES connects to entry barriers in Five Forces (S4).

slideExtras.detail: Small shop (1,000 pizzas/month): rent $10,000 + equipment $5,000 + ingredients $2,000 + labor $3,000 = $20,000 → $20.00/pizza. Large shop (10,000): $10,000 + $5,000 + $18,000 ($1.80, 10% bulk discount) + $24,000 ($2.40, 20% labor efficiency) = $57,000 → $5.70/pizza, 71.5% lower.

Q1 why didn't Blockbuster's 10x size protect it; Q2 fixed vs. variable for store, DVD-by-mail, streaming and which curve is steepest; Q3 why value flowed to content owners and what originals changed; Q4 how Netflix could outspend HBO 7x with lower cost per subscriber; Q5 is the advantage durable.

slideExtras.topic: Scale vs. learning in slide notes
slideExtras.detail: With scale, small and large firms can coexist if there's an efficient scale beyond which costs rise, or with differentiation; with learning-by-doing, the only cause of coexistence is differentiation (or a new firm hoping to move down the curve).

quant.what: Learning curve: s, b, doublings, unit cost, catch-up volume (Appendix A worked problems: $100→$64 over 1,000→4,000 units = 80%; 85% curve, $500,000 first unit → 64th unit $188,600; 500k-ton plant $200M → 1M tons $303M, capital/ton $400 → $303; follower $124k vs. leader $47k at 81.5% → 4.7 doublings ≈ 27x).
Fixed cost per subscriber F/N and breakeven N = F/(ARPU×12).

crossLinks402.note: 402's convention: fitted exponent b is negative and the cut per doubling is 2^b − 1. 401's brief writes Y = aX^−b with b positive and progress ratio s = 2^−b. Same math, opposite sign convention.
